\section[dadhi]{\sk{दधि} (dadhi) — curd}

\label{lesson:SA-C40-curd}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{sarpaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{दधि}}
\textbf{\sk{दधि}} (\emph{dadhi}) — \textquotedblleft{}curd\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{दधि}} is curd — \sk{दुग्धम्} set thick, the \emph{dahī} of every kitchen in India.

The word is a doubled thing: \emph{da-dh-i}, the root \emph{dhā}, \textquotedblleft{}to set, to place\textquotedblright{}, said twice over. Curd is milk that has been set, and the name says so twice for emphasis.

Hindi \emph{dahī}, Marathi \emph{dahī}, Gujarati \emph{dahī} — the word barely moved.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Milk, set thick.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dadhi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{sarpaḥ}, then \emph{dadhi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{दधि} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}curd\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śarkarā]{\sk{शर्करा} (śarkarā) — sugar}

\label{lesson:SA-C40-sugar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{dadhi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{शर्करा}}
\textbf{\sk{शर्करा}} (\emph{śarkarā}) — \textquotedblleft{}sugar\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{शर्करा}} is sugar, and before that it was grit and gravel — then the sweet grit that comes off boiled cane.

This one word is behind every sugar in Europe. It went into Arabic as \emph{sukkar}, into Latin as \emph{saccharum}, and from there into Italian \emph{zucchero}, French \emph{sucre}, German \emph{Zucker} and English \emph{sugar} and \emph{saccharine}.

Feminine, ending in \textbf{-\sk{आ}}, like \sk{माला} and \sk{शिला}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The Sanskrit word inside every European sugar.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{śarkarā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{dadhi}, then \emph{śarkarā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{शर्करा} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}sugar\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[navanītam]{\sk{नवनीतम्} (navanītam) — fresh butter}

\label{lesson:SA-C40-butter}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{śarkarā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{नवनीतम्}}
\textbf{\sk{नवनीतम्}} (\emph{navanītam}) — \textquotedblleft{}fresh butter\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{नवनीतम्}} is butter just off the churn, and both of its pieces are already yours.

The first piece, \emph{nava}, is \textquotedblleft{}new\textquotedblright{} — the word you learned beside \sk{महत्} and \sk{अल्प}. \emph{nīta} is \textquotedblleft{}brought, led\textquotedblright{}, from the same \emph{nī} that stands inside \sk{नयति}. Butter is the newly-brought thing — what has just been led up out of the \sk{दधि}.

It is the butter of the Kṛṣṇa stories, stolen by the handful, and Hindi \emph{navnīt} is still a name people give a child.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Butter, named as the new thing brought up out of the curd.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{navanītam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{śarkarā}, then \emph{navanītam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{नवनीतम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}fresh butter\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śākam]{\sk{शाकम्} (śākam) — a vegetable, a green}

\label{lesson:SA-C40-vegetable}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{navanītam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{शाकम्}}
\textbf{\sk{शाकम्}} (\emph{śākam}) — \textquotedblleft{}a vegetable, a green\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{शाकम्}} is a vegetable, and especially a leaf one — the cooked greens that a Hindi menu calls \sk{साग}.

Where \sk{पत्रम्} is the leaf on a \sk{लता}, \textbf{\sk{शाकम्}} is the leaf in a pot.

No cousin outside India has been agreed for it. The word stayed home, and it is doing the same work today it was doing three thousand years ago.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Leaves on the plant, and leaves in the pot.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{śākam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{navanītam}, then \emph{śākam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{शाकम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a vegetable, a green\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[modakaḥ]{\sk{मोदकः} (modakaḥ) — a sweet dumpling}

\label{lesson:SA-C40-sweet}



\begin{quote}
Before the last word of the chapter: what did \emph{navanītam} mean, and what did \emph{śākam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{मोदकः}}
\textbf{\sk{मोदकः}} (\emph{modakaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a sweet dumpling\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{मोदकः}} is a sweet — the round steamed dumpling put before a guest, and before a god.

It is built on \emph{mud}, \textquotedblleft{}to be glad\textquotedblright{}, so the name of the sweet is the name of the gladness it makes. \sk{आनन्दः}, the joy you offered at a first meeting, reaches for the same idea by a different root.

Set one in front of an \sk{अतिथिः} and the word does its own explaining.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five things from a kitchen: curd, sugar, butter, greens, a sweet.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{modakaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{dadhi} and \emph{modakaḥ} together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{मोदकः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a sweet dumpling\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
